books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, A. Religious and Spiritual Movements in Antebellum America

primary_sources: Charles G. Finney, "What a Revival of Religion Is" (Lectures on Revivals of Religion), 1835

stimulus.text: "When the churches are thus awakened and reformed, the reformation and salvation of sinners will follow.... Their hearts will be broken down and changed. Very often the most abandoned profligates are among the subjects. Harlots, and drunkards, and infidels, and all sorts of abandoned characters, are awakened and converted." — Charles G. Finney, "What a Revival of Religion Is," 1835
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Charles G. Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835), Lecture 1. Wording checked against the staged survivor barrons-2027-ch06-07 and the standard published text of the lecture.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Finney, Lectures on Revivals of Religion (1835)
stem: A historian using this passage as evidence would most likely argue that revival preaching in the 1830s did which of the following?

options.text: Kept religion a private matter by discouraging public displays of conversion
options.misconception: Religion feels private and inward, so a passage about hearts changing seems to point inward, not outward.

options.text: Strengthened the authority of established clergy by defending their control over church membership
options.misconception: Ministers wrote the passage, so it is easy to read it as ministers defending their own authority.

options.text: Turned Americans away from reform by teaching that only God could change society
options.misconception: The passage credits God with changing hearts, so it can look like human reform has no part to play.

options.text: Made conversion a public, emotional event that ordinary people joined and carried into reform

rationales.A: Finney's revivals were famously public: crowded meetings, anxious benches, and converts coming forward. Nothing here keeps conversion private.
rationales.B: Finney's methods challenged established clergy, who disliked his emotional tactics and his claim that revivals came from human effort. The passage weakens their control, not strengthens it.
rationales.C: Finney taught the opposite: revivals are produced by human effort as well as grace, and converted people were expected to reform society. The passage points toward reform, not away from it.
rationales.D: The passage parades converts in public, even the most abandoned characters. That public, emotional conversion is what revivalists then carried into temperance, abolition, and moral reform.
rationales.general:
1. Notice the stage: Finney describes conversions happening in front of a congregation, with named kinds of sinners.
2. Ask who is invited: everyone, even the most abandoned, so conversion is open to ordinary people.
3. Ask where the energy goes: converts left revivals to reform drinking, slavery, and vice.
Background: Finney taught that revivals were the product of human means, not only of divine will.
Remember: a public conversion is a recruit, and recruits become reformers.
